question_text: Explore how Webster presents death in The Duchess of Malfi.

rationale_2026: Last examined 2021, central concern of play. Ars Moriendi territory always exam-likely.
content_markdown:
Webster presents death as the dramatic instrument through which the corruption of the Italianate court is anatomised, and the trajectory tracks the deployment of differently weighted deaths — saintly, pathological, accidental, ceremonial — to expose the bankruptcy of every discourse the Jacobean stage had at its disposal for processing mortality. The Duchess's death constitutes the play's only authentic dramatisation of the *Ars Moriendi*, while the deaths that surround it progressively expose the corrupted court as a system in which death has been evacuated of its theological apparatus and converted into political instrument.

**[AO1 + AO2]** Webster establishes death's diagnostic function through Antonio's opening encomium of the French king, which establishes the normative civil-religious frame. **[AO2]** The image of the prince's court as a "common fountain" whose poisoning spreads "death and diseases through the whole land" pathologises mortality as the consequence of political corruption: deaths in Malfi are produced by the corrupted source, and the entire trajectory of the play unfolds as the literalisation of that opening medical-fluvial conceit. **[AO3]** For many in Webster's Blackfriars audience in 1613–14, the resonance was sharp. The Overbury affair of 1613 — in which Sir Thomas Overbury had died in the Tower by poisoning arranged by court favourites — had made political poisoning an immediately recognisable Jacobean scandal, and Webster's deployment of poison as the play's signature instrument of murder operates within that contemporary frame. Death is therefore presented as the dramatic literalisation of political pathology.

**[AO1 + AO2]** Webster's most refined dramatisation of death is the *Ars Moriendi* the Duchess constructs in 4.2. **[AO2]** The discipline required preparation through four stages: confession, contrition, resignation, and a calm composure of the dying body. Webster's stagecraft enacts each. The Duchess's preparation begins with her instruction to Cariola — "give my little boy / Some syrup for his cold, and let the girl / Say her prayers ere she sleep" — converting maternal labour into the play's most exact emblem of her domestic counter-court's persistence even in extremis. Her composition continues with the kneeling: "Heaven gates are not so highly arched / As princes' palaces; they that enter there / Must go upon their knees." Her assertion — "I am Duchess of Malfi still" — articulates the integrity of identity that the discipline required, and her last word — "Mercy!" — completes the *Ars Moriendi*'s requirement of resignation. **[AO3]** Many in Webster's audience would have recognised the *Ars Moriendi* tradition as belonging to the late-medieval Catholic discipline of dying well, partially retained in Protestant devotional culture. Death is therefore presented as the only register in which the corrupted court's apparatus can be transcended.

**[AO1 + AO2]** Webster's juxtaposition of Cariola's death immediately afterwards exposes the *Ars Moriendi* as a classed apparatus. **[AO2]** Cariola is granted no *Ars Moriendi*: she protests, fights, claims pregnancy ("I am quick with child"), demands confession ("Yet, save me till I have / Discoursed in private with the Duke"), and is strangled in panic. **[AO3]** Many in Webster's audience would have recognised the contrast between aristocratic Stoic dying and the panicked death of the servant as a Jacobean dramatic commonplace. While a traditionalist Christian reading sees the Duchess's death as the play's authentic spiritual dramatisation, a more historicist reading recognises Webster's stagecraft as exposing the *Ars Moriendi* as an aristocratic discipline available only to those whose social position has prepared them for it. The discipline is real; it is also classed.

**[AO1 + AO2]** Webster's most psychologically refined dramatic moment is Ferdinand's response to the Duchess's corpse. **[AO2]** His command to Bosola — "Cover her face; mine eyes dazzle: she died young" — is a single trimeter line that contains the entire collapse of the Aragonian apparatus into recognition of what it has destroyed. The verb "dazzle" is technically extraordinary: the eyes of the man who has orchestrated the murder cannot bear the sight of its accomplishment, and the brief assertion "she died young" registers the recognition that she has been killed before her natural span. While a generic reading sees Ferdinand's response as conventional villain's belated recognition, a more refined reading recognises Webster's stagecraft as permitting recognition without redemption. Ferdinand will collapse into lycanthropy almost immediately afterwards, the Doctor reporting in 5.2 that he "steals forth to churchyards in the dead of night, / And digs dead bodies up". The lycanthropy is a death-in-life that completes Webster's anatomy of the Aragonian pathology: the man who has killed his sister becomes the bestial figure who desecrates graves.

**[AO1 + AO2]** Webster stages Julia's death by poisoning in 5.2 as the play's most refined emblem of Counter-Reformation devotional perversion. **[AO2]** The Cardinal's poisoning of her with a kiss upon a sacred book is the play's exact inversion of the *Ars Moriendi*: where the Duchess died with sacramental composition, Julia dies in the act of swearing a perverted oath, and the kiss — the gesture of devotional adoration — is converted into the agent of murder. **[AO3]** Many in Webster's audience would have recognised the inversion within the Protestant polemical tradition: the Counter-Reformation devotional apparatus weaponised into an instrument of liquidation. The political resonance with the Overbury affair is also operative: Julia, like Overbury, dies because she has come to know too much. Death is therefore presented as the medium through which religious apparatus can be weaponised.

**[AO1 + AO2]** Webster's most economical political indictment is the Cardinal's death in 5.5. **[AO2]** His cries for help — "Help! help! I am betrayed" — are heard from the balcony by the courtiers whose function has been to ratify his *fama*, and they refuse to enter, commenting with icy parody: "Some falling-out amongst the cardinals … / He doth this very often." The scene exposes the corrupted court as a system in which the very sycophants whose service had authenticated the Cardinal's authority now ratify his death by refusing to interrupt their performance of it. His final self-acknowledgement — "I am puzzled in a question about hell" — registers the bankruptcy of an ecclesiastical career conducted without theological seriousness. Antonio's death in 5.4 is the play's most refined emblem of accidental mortality: Bosola, in mistaken identity, kills him in the theatrical darkness of the candle-lit stage, and the death's accidental character is its political argument — in a court where intention and outcome have come unmoored, even the play's moral protagonist dies by mistake.

**[AO1 + AO2]** Webster completes the trajectory through Bosola's death. **[AO2]** His closing line — "We are merely the stars' tennis-balls, struck and bandied / Which way please them" — articulates the post-providential fatalism that the corrupted court has produced, and the image of human agency as ball in the cosmic game registers the bankruptcy of the older Boethian theology of providence. While a Christian reading sees the Duchess's *Ars Moriendi* as the play's authentic theological dramatisation, a more sceptical reading recognises that Bosola's closing fatalism is the dramatic conclusion Webster permits the play to reach. The Duchess's death is real; so is its political insufficiency.

**[Conclusion linked to question]** Webster therefore presents death not as the spiritual culmination of life but as the operative instrument of the corrupted court's reproduction. The opening pathologised image of mortality as political consequence, the Duchess's *Ars Moriendi* as transcendent integrity, Cariola's panicked death as classed contrast, Ferdinand's recognition without redemption and collapse into lycanthropy, Julia's sacramental poisoning, the Cardinal's abandoned death, Antonio's accidental killing, and Bosola's fatalist conclusion together constitute Webster's typology of Jacobean mortality. The cumulative effect is to expose the political and theological apparatus available to the early modern subject as systematically inadequate to the reality of dying, and only the Duchess transcends it — at the cost of her life.
